CarveyanceThe Long View

Ninety-Three Years of the Soap Box Derby

CleanRacing

The most famous race nobody can name — and the one rule nobody has ever been able to engineer around.

By Margot Devries · 20 minute read

Let me describe a race, and you tell me which one it is.

It is one of the oldest and most famous races on the planet. It runs at the same time every year. It has drawn crowds north of a hundred thousand people. It has had marquee corporate sponsorship measured in millions of dollars a year, a genuine cheating scandal that made national news, a doping-adjacent controversy involving hidden electronics, celebrity grand marshals, two future U.S. presidents in the reviewing stand, an international circuit anchored in the United States and Germany, and a purpose-built permanent racing facility that has been in continuous operation since 1936. It was also, in 1991, given one of the most affectionate parodies in television history.

You have ten guesses. You will not get it.

It is the Soap Box Derby. Which is, when you sit with it for a second, genuinely absurd — this is a sport with more accumulated drama per capita than most professional racing series, and its entire competitive field is made up of children in unpowered wooden boxes rolling down a hill in Ohio. It has no engines. It has no fuel. Its fastest recorded run averages roughly twenty-five miles an hour, which is slower than a competent cyclist. And it has been doing this, with one four-year interruption for a world war and one for a pandemic, since Franklin Roosevelt's first term.

It started, as the best things do, with some kids in a backyard being kids.

One

How It Actually Started

On June 10, 1933, a 25-year-old staff photographer for the Dayton Daily News named Myron Scott was out on an ordinary assignment when he came across a handful of Dayton kids racing homemade carts down a hill. Scott, hunting material for the paper's Sunday picture page, saw a decent local story and told the boys to gather more of their friends and come back later that summer, when he would run a real race with real prizes.

He badly underestimated his own idea. The race went off on August 19, 1933, down steep, brick-paved Burkhardt Avenue, behind a full parade, and the turnout was staggering: better than 325 entries by the Dayton papers' count, 362 racers by another, all boys but one. Police estimated the crowd lining the street at more than 40,000 — a number worth pausing on, since Dayton's entire population at the time was around 200,000. Roughly one in five people in the city came to watch children roll down a hill in fruit crates. It was free, it was outdoors, and there was a parade, which in the summer of 1933 was a considerably better offer than it sounds.

The one entry who was not a boy was a girl named Alice Johnson. She finished second — a detail that becomes considerably more interesting about forty paragraphs from now.

Scott moved fast, copyrighting the concept himself. And the reason it caught fire is inseparable from the year it happened: in the depths of the Depression, a soap box car cost essentially nothing, which meant a kid with scrap lumber and cast-off wheels could line up dead even with his wealthier neighbor. It rewarded ingenuity rather than money, it fed America's growing obsession with the automobile, and it was free family entertainment at a moment when there was not much of that going around. Sponsors, newspapers, and parents all found something to love, which almost never happens.

A footnote on Myron Scott, who was having a remarkable life

Scott (1907–1998) spent 22 years at the Dayton Daily News, eventually as chief photographer and art director, before leaving for a three-decade career in Chevrolet's advertising and public relations department. Which brings us to his other claim to fame.

In 1953, when General Motors executives were stuck trying to name a new sports car, Scott went home, opened a dictionary to the Cs, and landed on “corvette” — a small, fast naval warship. He pitched it the next morning. It stuck. The same man invented the Soap Box Derby and named the Corvette, and if you are keeping a list of people who got more out of one lifetime than seems reasonable, add him.

Two

And Why “Soap Box,” Exactly?

Because that is literally what the cars were. Before there were rulebooks, kits, or sponsors, kids built racers out of whatever sturdy wooden crates they could scrounge, and the sturdiest, most plentiful, most reliably free crates behind any grocery store in America were the ones soap had shipped in. Bolt salvaged wheels to a soap crate and you have a soap box car. Race a few of them down a hill and you have a Soap Box Derby.

It is not a metaphor. It is not branding some agency workshopped over lunch. It is a description of the raw material, which tells you almost everything you need to know about the spirit of the thing.

Three

Going National: Chevrolet, Akron, and a New Deal Racetrack

Scott's idea scaled fast. Chevrolet signed on as national sponsor, and the first true All-American Soap Box Derby — a championship drawing local winners from around the country — ran on August 19, 1934, again in Dayton. Eleven-year-old Robert Turner of Muncie, Indiana took it by 1.4 seconds in a car built from the wood of an old bar and a set of stroller wheels, and left with $500 and a four-year college scholarship. Not a bad return on salvaged furniture.

In 1935 Akron's civic leaders lobbied hard to move the race to their city, pitching a more central location, better hills, and a promise from the local publisher to build the Derby a permanent home. They delivered. Construction on Derby Downs began in 1936, built with Works Progress Administration labor as a New Deal public-works project: a paved three-lane hill roughly 990 feet long, a staging area at the top, a run-out beyond the finish, and a two-deck wooden bridge over the finish line for spectators. It has been the sport's headquarters and the site of the World Championship ever since — which makes Derby Downs a ninety-year-old federal jobs-program project still performing its original function, daily, in the summer. There are not many of those left.

Four

The Golden Age, and Then the Trouble

The Derby ran every summer from 1934 through 1941 before going dark for four years during World War II, when rubber and metal were needed for less recreational purposes. It came back in 1946 to crowds reportedly north of 100,000, launching what is generally considered its golden age — Akron regularly pulling 50,000 to 70,000 spectators a year through the fifties and sixties, with genuine celebrity wattage in the grandstands. Jimmy Stewart came six times, more than any other guest. Ronald Reagan attended in 1951 as an actor and Richard Nixon in 1959 as vice president. Dale Earnhardt turned up in later years, which tells you how seriously people who drive for a living took this event.

Chevrolet, which had bankrolled the whole operation since 1934 at a peak of nearly a million dollars a year and roughly $1.7 million in cumulative scholarships, walked away on September 28, 1972. General manager John DeLorean reportedly considered it dated and expensive relative to other options, and the money went to America's Junior Miss and the Junior Olympics instead. Had DeLorean gotten around to building his time machine a decade sooner, one suspects he might have gone back and reconsidered. Chevrolet left a parting $30,000 toward the 1973 race, and the Akron Chamber of Commerce scrambled to keep the lights on with a fraction of the old budget.

Then 1973 happened, and the Soap Box Derby stopped being wholesome for about a week.

Five

The Sport Comes Clean

Fourteen-year-old Jimmy Gronen of Boulder, Colorado won the 1973 World Championship by margins of twenty to thirty feet, in a sport where a comfortable win is three feet and most heats are decided by less than one. Officials did what officials do when a result strains credulity: they X-rayed the car. Inside the nose they found a homemade electromagnet, wired to a switch in the headrest, which Gronen activated by pressing his head back at the start — giving the steel starting gate an extra magnetic tug on his car at precisely the moment it mattered.

He was stripped of the title within three days. Runner-up Bret Yarborough was declared champion, and Gronen forfeited a $7,500 scholarship. The scheme had been engineered by his uncle, Robert Lange, a former aerospace engineer, who was prosecuted and settled by agreeing to pay $2,000 to a local boys' club — a resolution that is either lenient or perfect, depending on your view of aerospace engineers.

The story broke while the country was already marinating in Watergate, which is genuinely unfortunate timing for anyone hoping to keep a children's event out of the national conversation about cheating. And it forced a reckoning: a sport whose entire premise was homemade fairness had to prove it could police itself.

One kid's electromagnet permanently rewrote how the entire sport operates.A hell of a legacy for a thirteen-dollar science project

What came out of it is, more or less, the modern rulebook. In 1974 the Derby adopted a double-elimination format in which competitors swap lanes and swap wheel sets between runs, so no single lane, wheel, or hidden gadget can decide a race. By 1976 it had introduced standardized kit cars — uniform shells, wheels, and axles supplied directly by the organization. Fifty years later every division races on standardized components and every car is weighed and inspected before every heat.

Six

Which Brings Us, Inevitably, to The Simpsons

If all of that sounds like the plot of a cartoon, there is a reason it feels familiar. Season 3 of The Simpsons contains an episode called “Saturdays of Thunder” (1991) built entirely around a soap box derby, and it remains the most accurate portrait of the sport's competitive psychology ever committed to film — animated or otherwise.

Homer, attempting to bond with Bart, helps him build a racer that is, charitably, not good. Bart promptly defects to Martin Prince's entry instead: a sleek, aerodynamically engineered machine bristling with functional switches and knobs and fitted with an actual working parachute, which deploys — memorably — after the crash rather than before it. And then Nelson Muntz arrives in the “Roadkill 2000,” rigged with enough illegal hardware to hospitalize a modern tech inspector.

Which is the joke, and also not a joke. Standardized kits, mandatory pre-race inspection, and the lane-and-wheel swap all exist precisely because somebody actually ran the Nelson Muntz strategy in 1973 and very nearly got away with it. The writers were not exaggerating the sport. They were reporting on it.

For the completists, there is also a 1958 British film simply called Soapbox Derby, notable mostly for featuring a fifteen-year-old Michael Crawford in his first screen appearance.

Seven

Girls Take the Wheel

Here is a rule that never technically existed: no Derby rulebook ever barred girls from competing. In practice they were shut out for nearly four decades anyway, because Chevrolet dealerships sold the mandatory wheel-and-axle sets and a good number of them simply declined to sell to girls or accept their entries. A rule you can point to is easier to fight than a rule everybody just quietly follows.

It gave way in 1971, under pressure from the Women's Liberation Movement, and girls were officially welcomed. Rebecca Carol Phillips of Temple, Texas became the first girl to officially run the Akron hill that year, and won her opening heat, which is a fairly emphatic way to make a point. Four years later, eleven-year-old Karren Stead of Lower Bucks County, Pennsylvania became the first female World Champion — driving, and this is the part that should be on a poster, with her arm in a cast from an injury sustained days earlier at Derby camp. In 1994 Danielle Del Ferraro became the first two-time champion in Derby history of any gender.

And Alice Johnson, the lone girl in that very first 1933 Dayton field, had finished second thirty-eight years before any of it was allowed.

Interlude

Saturday Morning, Summer of 1939

Set the record books aside for a minute, because none of the above is what the Soap Box Derby actually was to the hundred thousand kids who never got within a thousand miles of Akron. For them it looked like this.

You are twelve, which means you are — at this exact moment — the most important engineer in the free world. Your laboratory is your father's garage. Your materials are whatever the neighborhood has not nailed down: a wagon wheel with three good spokes, half a fence post, a roller skate sacrificed for its bearings, and a length of clothesline your mother will notice missing eventually. Under the floorboard, held on with a fistful of rusty nails and pure optimism, is a brake — a hinged wooden block that will, theoretically, drag on the pavement and slow you down. Nobody has tested it. Nobody wants to be the one who finds out. By any reasonable engineering standard the whole thing is a catastrophe, and you love it with your entire chest.

Race day. You haul it to the steepest hill in town, because obviously that is the only appropriate venue for a World Championship. Somebody's older brother drops a red bandana as the starting flag, primarily because he wants to see a crash. The finish line, seventy yards down, is Mrs. McCray's mailbox.

For the first ten feet everything is perfect and you are speed itself. For the next twenty you notice a sound the car has never made before, a rhythmic high shriek, as though the axle has developed opinions. By thirty feet you cannot hear anything at all — just wind and gravel and your own pulse — and glory is fifty feet out and closing. Which is precisely when your left front wheel, the good one, the one you babied all summer, resigns from the project and pursues a trajectory of its own. You counter-steer. You do everything right. It changes nothing. The car, now down twenty-five percent of its wheels and roughly sixty percent of its dignity, bounces off the curb and deposits you at an entirely unnecessary rate of speed into Mrs. McCray's prize thorn bushes.

You lost the race. You also got a scar you are already planning to describe very differently at school on Monday, and the finest wipeout the block has ever witnessed. And you learned something the hard way that the sport would spend the next fifty years engineering out of existence: a wheel that is not properly attached will find its own way home.

Eight

The Cars: From Soap Crates to Composites

One rule has never changed, not once, in ninety-three years: gravity only. No motors, no engines, no assistance of any kind. Every car has four wheels, and every ounce of speed comes from the hill, the car's weight distribution, and how well it was built and steered. That is the whole sport.

Everything else has been reinvented from the ground up. The earliest cars were genuinely improvised — scrap wood, salvaged roller-skate or baby-carriage wheels, a rope tied to the front axle for steering, and a hinged wooden block dragged against the pavement for braking. Which means the Soap Box Derby was running a functional Lever 2000 roughly two millennia ahead of schedule, and nobody has ever given it credit.

By the mid-1930s Chevrolet dealerships sold an official standardized wheel-and-axle set, though bodies stayed home-built and wooden for decades. Fiberglass broke through in 1962, when David Mann won the World Championship in an early fiberglass-shelled car, and through the sixties and seventies builders increasingly sheathed wood-strip frames in fiberglass and epoxy the way you would build a canoe. Metal wheels, which had become expensive to manufacture, gave way in 1982 to fiberglass-reinforced nylon — the long-serving “Z-Glas” wheel, which did add a certain Zest to the proceedings, since replaced by a newer “UniGrip” design. In 1999 the Masters division, the last holdout still building from scratch, moved to a standardized kit, completing the sport's long march from scrappy improvisation to squeaky-clean uniformity.

Today's cars come out of an organization-supplied kit: a composite shell engineered for aerodynamics, pre-approved wheels, a standard axle assembly, a mandatory inspected brake, and a standardized steering mechanism. Reasonable people can debate whether that trade was worth it, and Derby families absolutely do.

Who Can Race

Eligibility runs from age 7 to 20, split across four divisions by age, driver size, and car design. Combined weight — car plus driver plus wheels — is capped by division, and racers under the cap add ballast to reach it, which is how a 65-pound kid and a 120-pound kid end up racing on genuinely even terms.

The four divisions
DivisionAgesBody styleNotes
Stock7–13Open cockpit, sit-upEntry-level kit; car + driver capped near 200 lb
Super Stock9–18Open cockpit, sit-upBigger sibling of Stock; cap near 240 lb
Masters10–20Enclosed, lay-downMost advanced standard division; cap near 255 lb
Legacy12–20Open invitationAkron Race Week only; for experienced racers

Legacy is the interesting one: it runs only during Race Week in Akron, is never contested locally, and exists for experienced racers applying aerodynamic and chassis thinking well beyond what a standard kit allows — the closest thing the Derby has to an engineering open class.

Nine

What Happens When You Take the Kit Away

That trade-off — the standardized composite shell against the last of the salvaged-fence-post spirit — actually has a real-world answer, and it did not happen in Akron.

In 2000, a Southern California event organizer named Don MacAllister staged a small charity race pairing homemade gravity cars with a jobs program he had just founded for foster kids, called America Works for Kids. MacAllister knew the territory personally; he has said the organization grew directly out of his own experience aging out of foster care at eighteen with no real support system behind him. That first race borrowed the Derby's basic shape without asking anyone's permission: four wheels, no engine, a hill, some kids.

By 2003 word had reached the design studios, and the whole thing mutated fast. Porsche and Mazda faced off that year in an exhibition MacAllister branded Extreme Gravity Racing, and Porsche's in-house entry — a sleek car called the Soapboard, its name punning soap box against surfboard, styled after Southern California surf culture — won outright. The following year General Motors' own design staff took the win with a car nicknamed the Flying Shoe. Bentley entered the Crewes Missile, a black bomber styled after the actual Bentley Speed 8 that had won Le Mans the year before. Nissan, Volvo, Chrysler, Volkswagen, Audi, and Pininfarina all fielded entries within a few seasons, built for the studios by a specialty fabricator called 3dyn. By 2007, under the rebranded banner Zero Emission Racing Cup, Aston Martin's design director Marek Reichman was personally penning the company's third gravity racer from inside its Warwick studio.

MacAllister was explicit that this was not the Soap Box Derby's little cousin, and the numbers back him up. His cars ran roughly nine feet long and four feet wide against the Derby's six-by-two, down courses up to half a mile long with real curves in them rather than a 200-foot straightaway, hitting 60 to 70 mph where a strong Derby run tops out in the high twenties. “This is the adult version,” he told one reporter. Reported build costs ran from around $30,000 for early cars up to something like $100,000 once design-studio research and development time was factored in; a handful of the finished cars have separately sold at charity auction for as much as $60,000.

And they were fast in exactly the way you would expect professional design studios and an unlimited budget to be fast: aluminum and carbon-fiber bodywork, real aerodynamic development, functioning brakes rather than a block dragged against the pavement. The series pulled in university engineering teams too — UC Irvine's graduate and undergraduate students won a Most Innovative Car award at a 2006 running on Malibu's twisting Tuna Canyon Road, where cars were capped at 350 pounds combined and still reached 50 mph.

Nobody appears to have organized a race after one scheduled for August 2008, and the timing is hard to read as coincidence. The surviving cars mostly live in private collections now — museum placards instead of race results.

Keep the one rule about gravity. Strip away every restriction the Derby spent ninety-three years adding. What is left is faster. What is missing is the kid.The experiment, run in reverse
Ten

How a Race Actually Works

Nobody just shows up in Akron. A racer builds a car, usually across several weekends with a parent or mentor elbow-deep in it, then races locally or at a rally in one of twelve U.S. rally districts (there is an International district as well). Points accumulate across a season running June 1 to May 31; local champions and top point-scorers earn invitations to the World Championship each July. It is a genuine nationwide pipeline — well over a thousand sanctioned local and rally races a year, more than eighty licensed race cities, funneling 500-plus qualifiers from more than forty states and several countries into a single week.

Race day runs on double elimination, and the twist is the whole point. Lose once and you drop into the consolation bracket; racers have fought all the way back from there to win. But each “heat” is actually two runs between the same two competitors: after the first pass, the drivers swap lanes and swap wheel sets, then go again, with combined time deciding it. That single mechanism — born directly out of 1973 — means no lane advantage, no wheel advantage, and nowhere for a hidden gadget to hide. It comes down to the car and the kid, which is what it was supposed to be about in the first place.

Eleven

Speed, Such As It Is

These are unpowered cars starting from a dead stop and coasting somewhere between 950 and 990 feet, which means “speed” is really a proxy for weight distribution, axle friction, aerodynamics, and driver technique. It is a physics exam that happens to be thrilling, which is precisely why the modern organization leans on it as a STEM program.

Track records by era
Track eraLengthRecord holderTimeYear

2000–present989.4 ftSherry Lazowski (Ultimate Speed)26.5852011

Look at that table for a second, because it is quietly the most remarkable thing in this article. Derby Downs has been resurfaced, reconfigured, and re-measured four times, so the records are era-specific rather than cumulative — but line up the times anyway. In 1939 the fastest run was 27.80 seconds. In 1947, 26.63. In 1974, 27.10. In 2004, 28.24. Nine decades of materials science, aerodynamics, and precision manufacturing separate the first from the last, and the times have gone essentially nowhere. Tony Penuelas set a mark in 1947, using wheels bought at a Chevrolet dealership, that the sport has spent nearly eighty years failing to meaningfully improve on.

Average speeds land around 25 mph, which undersells the experience: the car accelerates the entire way down, so terminal speed at the finish line is considerably higher, with competitive Masters runs commonly described in the high twenties to mid thirties.

Twelve

The German Connection

The Derby is not purely American, and its largest foreign outpost has a distinctly postwar origin: American soldiers popularized the sport in the U.S. occupation zone after World War II. Berlin held its first Seifenkisten-Rennen on July 16, 1949, and a national German championship — the Deutsches Seifenkisten Derby — took shape in the same period, initially under U.S. Armed Forces sponsorship before Opel took over as national sponsor in 1951. Within a decade more than two hundred German communities were sending local champions to the national final, whose winner represented Germany at Akron. The program is still running today across four classes of its own, which makes the Soap Box Derby one of remarkably few American inventions Germany adopted and then simply kept. Canada, Japan, and New Zealand have sent champions to Akron too, but Germany remains the sport's second home by a wide margin.

Thirteen

Is It Still Going? Yes, and It Just Finished

The Derby has run continuously since 1946 with exactly one interruption — 2020, canceled for COVID-19, only the second cancellation in its history after the war years. The 88th FirstEnergy All-American Soap Box Derby World Championship ran at Derby Downs during Race Week in mid-July 2026 and has just wrapped. Amos Miller, 13, of Stanwood, Washington took the Stock world title; Alicia Swinderman of Rittman, Ohio won Super Stock; and Melvin Spoelstra, 13, of New Sharon, Iowa won Masters.

Which is to say: this week, three thirteen-year-olds became world champions in the same sport that crowned its first one when Roosevelt was in office, on the same hill, under the same one rule about gravity. That is a strange and rather wonderful piece of continuity for a competition most adults could not name if you gave them ten guesses.

Fourteen

The Point

It would be easy to file the Soap Box Derby under nostalgia — a sepia-toned thing that happened to your grandfather, kept alive by volunteers out of stubbornness. That reading is wrong, and the reason is the one rule nobody has ever been able to engineer around.

Every other form of racing has spent the last century in an arms race with its own rulebook. Budgets escalate, technology escalates, and the sport becomes, gradually, a competition between engineering departments with drivers attached. The Soap Box Derby cannot do that, because you cannot buy more gravity. The hill in Akron is the same hill it was in 1936, and the winning times have barely moved in ninety years — not because nobody has tried, but because the ceiling is physics, and physics is not accepting sponsorship dollars.

What is left, when you strip out horsepower and money, is a kid who spent six weekends in a garage with someone who loves them, learning that weight distribution is real and that axles must be straight and that the difference between winning and Mrs. McCray's thorn bushes is often a single overlooked detail. That was the entire idea in 1933, and it is somehow still the entire idea now.

The ISBD race locator will point you at a local Derby most summer weekends, in more than half the states in the country, run by volunteers, free to watch. Go stand at the bottom of the hill. No thorn bushes required, though no promises either.

Ninety-three years, two cancellations, one electromagnet, and not one engine.Clean racing, in every sense that matters
